concept: Heap sort builds a max heap from the input array, then repeatedly extracts the maximum (swap root with the last unsorted element, shrink the heap, siftDown) — each extraction places one more value in its final sorted position at the end of the array.
Building the initial heap is O(n), and each of the n extractions costs O(log n), giving O(n log n) overall in every case — no worst-case blowup like quick sort has.
Its other selling point is space: heap sort sorts in place, using O(1) extra memory, where merge sort's guaranteed O(n log n) comes at the cost of O(n) auxiliary space.
1.analogy: Repeatedly picking the tallest person from a crowd and moving them to the back of a line, one at a time. Once everyone's been picked, the line is sorted shortest-to-tallest from front to back.
1.mascotDialogue: Build the heap once, then just keep pulling the max off the top. Each pull is one more element locked into its correct final spot.

2.mascotDialogue: Two loops: build the heap once (lines 2-3), then repeatedly swap-and-shrink (lines 5-7). The 'end' bound shrinking each time is what carves out the sorted region at the back.

3.mascotDialogue: Watch the tallest bar get walked to the top, then swapped to the far right — that's one value locked into its sorted home.

4.bugDescription: Without calling siftDown after each swap, the shrinking region at the front never gets re-heapified. Only the very first extraction happens to be correct by luck of the initial heap; every extraction after that pulls from a broken heap and produces an incorrectly ordered result.
4.mascotDialogue: This is the one step that's easy to forget because the array still *changes* each loop — it just doesn't converge into sorted order without it.

5.question: Heap sort is generally described as which category of sorting algorithm?
5.answer: Comparison-based, O(n log n), in-place, not stable
hints: Every step compares parent vs. child values.
It sorts within the original array without extra storage proportional to n.
5.solution: Heap sort is a comparison-based, in-place algorithm with O(n log n) time complexity in all cases, but it is not stable — equal elements can end up reordered relative to each other.
